transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess it’s my eating. After late shifts, I’ll stop for takeout and it turns into a lot — like two burgers, fries, a shake — and then I still go home and eat leftovers out in the garage, like I’m having a whole second supper. It’s been bothering me.
When you're eating all that food, do you feel like you can't stop or control yourself once you start?

Yeah. Once I start, it’s like a switch gets flipped. I’ll be telling myself, “Roy, close the bag, go inside,” but my hands just keep reaching for more anyway. It doesn’t feel like I’m really in control of it.
Does this pattern of eating bother you a lot or cause problems in your life, like with your health, work, or relationships?

Yeah, it bothers me. I’m still making it to work and I keep up with church, so it’s not like everything’s fallen apart. But at home I’ve been pulling back some. I spend a lot of energy trying to cover up where I stopped for food or why I’m not hungry at dinner, and that gets tiring.
Do you feel ashamed or upset about these eating episodes after they happen?

Yeah. Afterward I feel pretty ashamed, honestly. Kind of disgusted with myself. I’ve always thought of myself as a disciplined, dependable guy, and then I’m out there sneaking food and hiding it. It makes me feel like I’m letting myself down.
After these eating episodes, do you ever try to compensate for the food you’ve eaten, like by making yourself sick, using laxatives, or exercising a lot more than usual?
No, not really. I don’t make myself sick or take laxatives or anything like that. I might tell myself I’ll “do better tomorrow,” but I’m not going out and exercising a bunch to make up for it.
Do these large eating episodes happen within a short period of time, like over the course of a couple of hours, or does it stretch out over a longer time, like several hours or more?

It’s usually pretty short, yeah. Like after a late shift I’ll stop for takeout, and I can put away two burgers, fries, a shake… then go home and eat leftovers out in the garage like it’s a second supper. That all happens in the same evening, pretty close together.

latest_inference.note: The patient's eating episodes occur in a short period of time, involve loss of control, and are followed by feelings of shame and self-disgust. There is no compensatory behavior. These features align more closely with F50.01 (Binge Eating Disorder) rather than F50.00 (Anorexia Nervosa), which has been ruled out due to absence of restrictive eating or fear of weight gain.
